The whole design chain for our own small VTOL quadplane (4 lift motors on two booms + 1 pusher, 2.24 m wing, 6S6P Li-ion): requirements -> mass and CG (from the CAD) -> airfoil -> drag buildup -> cruise aero -> hover thrust -> pusher thrust -> mission energy -> battery choice -> structure/stability checks -> electronics -> bill of materials and cost -> ways to cut cost -> decisions and why -> open checks.

Fly over chaparral at dawn and at midday carrying our own sensors (thermal + a 1610 nm water-band sensor), to measure how much water shrubs lose during the day for prescribed-burn planning. Our sensor kit is light (~0.3-0.45 kg), so the aircraft can be small and cheap.
Yellow cells = typed inputs, each with its source. Blue cells = formulas on other cells (click a cell to see the formula). Green cells = key results. Change a yellow input and every result updates.

The legal limit is sight, not distance; ~1 km is what we can reliably see a 2.2 m aircraft. Flying farther needs a BVLOS waiver.
Range on one charge is tens of km (Mission_Energy), far beyond the ~1 km we may fly. So the motors and battery are sized by hover thrust and by time on site for the day's flights, not by distance.
One dawn flight and one midday flight over the same plants need time to cover a hillside plot and hover for the spot sensor; 80 min kept even with a draggier airframe.
Below ~1.5 a quadplane cannot hold attitude in gusts while hovering at full mass. 800 m covers the hills around Stanford (Jasper Ridge < 300 m) with margin.
VTOL takes off and lands on rotors, so stall matters for transitions and slow turns, not landing. Lower stall = slower, safer transitions.
